newsitem.title: USA: Brazil bean crop cut to 26.3 mln tonnes-US attache.
newsitem.headline: Brazil bean crop cut to 26.3 mln tonnes-US attache.

text.p: Brazil's estimated soybean production for marketing year 1997 (Feb/Jan) was revised downward to 26.3 tonnes, based on 11.8 million hectares of planted fields, according to a report by a U.S. agricultural attache made public on Tuesday.

The report, dated June 30 and prepared by the U.S. embassy in Sao Paulo, said the 1 percent cut in estimated production would still leave Brazil with a record harvest, topping marketing year 1996 by almost 11 percent.
The average yield for the crop is estimated at about 2.23 tons per hectare, the report said.

The reduction in estimated soybean production for MY1997 is mainly related to a much lower than expected harvest in the state of Rio Grande do Sul because of a drought. The attache report lowered its production estimate for the state to 4.8 million tonnes, down almost 1 percent from the previous estimate.

With analysts' consensus for the initial production estimate to be in the range 5.8 to 6 million tons, this is the second straight year that bad weather has lowered the soybean harvest below the 5 million ton level and stripped Rio Grande do Sul of its leadership position in soybean production, the report said.

Soybean exports for MY1997 are now placed at 8 million tons, up 14 percent from the embassy's last estimate and over 116 percent higher than soybean shipments during MY1996, the report said. The main reasons for the surge in exports are high international prices, the removal of a value-added tax, and a halt to a tax differential which crushers previously had on exports of soybean meal and oil.
The Brazilian Oilseeds Crushers Association estimated the total value of soybean exports for MY1997 at more than US$2.4 billion dollars, up over 142 percent from MY1996.
As of June 15, over 7.847 million tons of soybeans had been registered for export with the Brazilian government, the report said.

The soybean crush for MY1997 was estimated at 18.3 million tons, down less than 4 percent from the last MY1997 estimate, but almost 9 percent lower than the MY1996 crush, the report said. The rise in soybean exports is the main reason for the sharp decline, the report said.

"The Brazilian oilseeds crushing industry is alarmed at this development and some of its members have advocated the placement of a tax on soybean exports to undercut these shipments," the report said. "So far, however, the Brazilian Government has demurred, since the revenues generated by soybean exports are one of the key forces in lowering its ballooning trade deficit."
To help compensate for the lowered soybean crush, Brazil is expected to import a record volume of soybeans -- 1.6 million tonnes, up 23 percent from MY1996, the report said.
Attache reports are not official USDA data.
